title: OAuth2 core endpoints (oauth/): authorization-server core, token stores, device grant, client registry

findings.title: An approved device_code is redeemable repeatedly: every poll mints a fresh token pair instead of consuming the device authorization
findings.why: PollDeviceAuthorization never invalidates or consumes the approved device record. Once a record reaches DeviceApproved, every later poll falls through the switch and calls s.issue again, minting a brand-new access+refresh pair (each in a brand-new family, because familyID is ""). RFC 8628 requires the device_code to be single-use after it has been exchanged for tokens; here it stays redeemable for the full DeviceCodeTTL (10 minutes by default). A leaked or replayed device_code keeps producing credentials, and because each issuance opens a new rotation family, a later replay/revocation of one family does not contain the others.
findings.exploit: A malicious or compromised device (or anyone who observed the device_code, e.g. from a request log or an installed app) calls POST /oauth/token with grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code and the approved device_code once every DevicePollInterval for the remaining TTL. Each call returns a new, valid access+refresh pair for the approving user. A burst of N concurrent polls is worse: each request reads rec.LastPoll before any RecordPoll write lands, so all N pass the slow_down check and all N mint. Revoking the user's grant through RevokeGrant still works because it scans by subject+client, but the per-family replay detection (RFC 9700) never connects these independent families.
findings.recommendation: Make the approved redemption atomic and single-use. After a successful decision, either delete the record in the store when the tokens are minted (add a ConsumeDevice/RecordRedemption store method that deletes only on DeviceApproved and returns false to the losing concurrent poller), or record a RedemptionNonce and refuse a second issue. Do not rely on the record expiring: the TTL is not single-use. A losing concurrent poll must receive invalid_grant, not a second token pair.

findings.title: MemoryDeviceStore never prunes pending/decided device records and exposes no sweep API, so device authorizations grow unbounded
findings.evidence:
func (s *MemoryDeviceStore) SaveDevice(_ context.Context, deviceCode string, d DeviceAuthorizationRecord) error {
	d.DeviceCodeHash = TokenHash(deviceCode)

	s.mu.Lock()
	defer s.mu.Unlock()
	s.byDev[d.DeviceCodeHash] = d
	s.byUser[NormalizeUserCode(d.UserCode)] = d.DeviceCodeHash
	return nil
}
findings.why: SaveDevice inserts into byDev and byUser and nothing in the package ever deletes from either map: MemoryDeviceStore has no delete, no expiry sweep and no SweepExpired counterpart to MemoryStore.SweepExpired. Expiry is enforced only on read. Every BeginDeviceAuthorization therefore permanently adds one record to each map. BeginDeviceAuthorization only needs a registered client id (describeScopes calls s.client(..., auth=false), so public clients need no secret), making the endpoint a cheap unauthenticated-ish allocation sink wherever a deployment mounts it without a hard rate cap. The oauth package itself defaults to this store (Config.Devices == nil -> NewMemoryDeviceStore), so a wiring that forgets to inject a DeviceStore silently gets an unbounded leak, and because DeviceStore has no pruning method at all, even a diligent embedder cannot bound it.
findings.exploit: An attacker repeatedly POSTs the device_authorization endpoint with a known public client_id. Each request allocates a 43-char device code plus a user code and two map entries that are never reclaimed, even after the 10-minute deadline passes. Sustained at the rate limiter's budget this grows process memory monotonically until OOM; a restart is the only reclamation.
findings.recommendation: Add a SweepExpired(now time.Time) int to MemoryDeviceStore (mirroring MemoryStore.SweepExpired) that deletes byDev entries past ExpiresAt and the corresponding byUser keys, document that DeviceStore implementations need pruning, and call it from a janitor loop. At minimum, have the default store bound its own size so the leak cannot be reached by forgetting configuration.

findings.title: MemoryStore.ConsumeRefresh ignores the tombstone deadline, so expired spent refresh values still trigger family revocation while the Postgres store correctly reports them unknown
findings.why: The tombstone carries ExpiresAt and the struct comment promises it 'expires on the spent token's own deadline', but ConsumeRefresh never reads tomb.ExpiresAt; any tombstone still resident in the map is reported as *RefreshReuseError regardless of age. The only remover is the manual SweepExpired, which nothing in this package calls, and the package documentation explicitly tolerates not sweeping. The Postgres implementation of the same oauth.Store method does enforce the deadline (WHERE token_hash = $1 AND expires_at > $2), so the two shipped stores disagree about a security-relevant signal, and the service maps that signal straight to destructive action: Refresh treats *RefreshReuseError as theft and calls RevokeRefreshFamily, killing every live descendant of the family. So an expired, already-spent value is misreported as a live replay and can revoke a still-valid generation of the same family that has a later deadline (family is inherited across rotations).
findings.exploit: A client rotates RT1 -> RT2 on day 1 (RT1 expires day 30, RT2 day 31). Nothing sweeps tombstones. On day 30.5 whoever holds the old RT1 (the legitimate client's own stale copy, a backup, or a leaked value) presents it to POST /oauth/token. MemoryStore returns *RefreshReuseError, oauth.Refresh calls RevokeRefreshFamily(RT1.FamilyID), and RT2 - the live session the user is still using - is deleted. The same value against the Postgres store would return invalid_grant and revoke nothing. A second, more common trigger: an expired current refresh token is spent on the first retry (error 'expired') and revokes the family on the immediate retry, producing a spurious theft alarm and audit record.
findings.recommendation: In MemoryStore.ConsumeRefresh, consult the tombstone deadline the same way Postgres does, e.g. compare tomb.ExpiresAt against time.Now() (or give the store a clock) and return ErrTokenNotFound when it has passed, so expired values are 'never issued' and never produce a reuse signal. Alternatively make SweepExpired mandatory and remove the 'accept the growth' escape, but the store must not depend on an out-of-package timer for a security decision.

findings.title: Token issuance is not atomic: a failure after SaveAccess leaves a live, undeliverable access token in the store
findings.why: issue writes the access token and then the refresh token with no transaction and no rollback. If SaveRefresh fails (a database error, a constraint, a timeout), the caller receives an error and never learns the access-token value, yet the record remains live for AccessTokenTTL and Introspect/Authenticate accept it. The store now holds a credential nobody can present, that cannot be tied to a delivered token, and that is only cleanable via the coarse subject+client revocation path. The mirror failure (SaveAccess fails) is clean because no record was written.
findings.exploit: Not directly attacker-triggerable, but a transient store failure (e.g. pool exhaustion under load) silently accumulates live orphan tokens that inflate the token tables and any grants-wide scan, and that count against family bloat. In a deployment relying on the returned TokenResponse as the only record of issuance there is no way to identify the orphan.
findings.recommendation: Make issuance atomic in the Store: one SaveTokenPair(ctx, atValue, at, rtValue, rt) that writes both rows in one transaction (or, for the memory store, under one lock), so a partial write cannot survive. If a pair API is too invasive, delete the just-written access token on SaveRefresh failure (delete-on-error) so the failure path leaves no live record.

findings.title: Client authentication tells an unknown client apart from a wrong secret, contradicting the kit's stated indistinguishability requirement
findings.why: The two failure branches return different Description strings ("unknown client" vs "invalid client credentials") on the same invalid_client code. upstreamkit's writeProtocolError serialises oe.Description verbatim into error_description, and the comment at upstreamkit/server.go:341-342 states the opposite property: 'an unauthenticated caller must not reach the hook, and must not be able to tell an unknown client from a bad secret.' There is also a timing difference (one map lookup vs a SHA-256 plus constant-time compare), so the oracle survives even if the text is unified. The result is reliable client-id enumeration against every endpoint that calls client(..., true): token, revoke, cascade revocation and AuthenticateClient.
findings.exploit: POST /oauth/token with Authorization: Basic base64(<guessed-id>:x) repeatedly. A response saying 'unknown client' means the id is not registered; 'invalid client credentials' means it is. The attacker enumerates registered downstream clients (useful for targeting the device_authorization endpoint, which needs no secret, and for the cascade-revocation path below).
findings.recommendation: Return one description for both branches ("invalid client credentials") from s.client, and make the unknown-client path perform a dummy constant-time comparison against a fixed digest so the timing does not distinguish them. Keep the distinction only in server-side logs.

findings.title: AuthenticateClient treats public clients as always authenticated, so the cascade-revocation gate does not actually gate public clients
findings.why: client(..., auth=true) only verifies a secret when c.Type == ClientConfidential. For a public client the supplied secret is ignored and the call succeeds unconditionally. upstreamkit handles POST /oauth/cascade_revocation by first calling AuthenticateClient and only then invoking the destructive CascadeRevoke hook (which ends the subject's whole upstream session), stating that the identity check 'cannot be left to each hook'. For public clients there is no identity check at all, so any caller who knows a registered public client id - trivially obtainable with S01-5 - reaches the hook. The hook then resolves the subject from the supplied token, so the only remaining barrier is the hook's own token validation, which the kit explicitly said it would not rely on.
findings.exploit: An attacker who holds any still-valid token value for a source (e.g. a stolen access token) and a public client id registered at that source POSTs the token to /oauth/cascade_revocation with that client_id and an arbitrary client_secret. AuthenticateClient returns nil, the hook runs, and the victim is signed out of every device at the upstream source - a denial of service the kit's own comment claims is prevented. Confidence is medium because the actual outcome depends on the embedder's hook implementation; the missing client authentication in the oauth core is certain.
findings.recommendation: Either refuse cascade revocation for public clients (return ErrNoSecretToRotate-like behaviour: the capability requires a confidential client), or make the endpoint authenticate with a method a public client can actually satisfy (proof of possession of the token that names the session, i.e. verify token ownership against the same client id before invoking the hook inside the kit rather than inside the hook). Document on AuthenticateClient that public clients are always accepted.

findings.title: RotateSecret accepts a hash of any length while RestoreClient demands sha256.Size, so a bad rotation silently locks a confidential client out
findings.why: RotateSecret validates only len(secretHash) != 0, but Authenticate compares c.secretHash against sha256.Sum256(secret) with subtle.ConstantTimeCompare, which returns 0 whenever the lengths differ. A hash that is not 32 bytes (e.g. a truncated or base64-encoded digest passed by an admin integration) therefore makes every subsequent authentication fail permanently, and the registry has no way to detect it at write time. RestoreClientWithStatus enforces exactly this invariant for the load path ('len(secretHash) != sha256.Size'), so the two paths disagree about what a valid stored digest is. The MemoryClientRegistry is used by tests and any embedder; persistent registries that follow the same interface inherit the risk unless they validate independently.
findings.exploit: Operator error or a buggy admin tool calls RotateSecret with a hex-encoded digest (64 bytes) instead of the raw 32-byte NewSecretHash output. The rotation reports success and the client secret is returned to the operator, but the client can never authenticate again and every request it makes fails with invalid_client; the only recovery is another rotation.
findings.recommendation: Validate len(secretHash) == sha256.Size in RotateSecret (and document the raw-digest contract on ClientAdmin.RotateSecret / NewSecretHash), matching RestoreClientWithStatus, so an invalid digest is rejected before it is persisted.

findings.title: Revoke cannot reach a spent refresh token's tombstone: the documented DeleteRefresh tombstone-clear is unreachable and RFC 7009 revocation of a rotated token is a false success
findings.evidence:
owner, err := s.tokens.TokenOwner(ctx, req.Token)
	switch {
	case errors.Is(err, ErrTokenNotFound):
		return nil
	case err != nil:
		return err
	case owner != client.ID:
		return nil
	}
findings.why: TokenOwner only consults the live access and refresh maps; a value that ConsumeRefresh already spent lives only in the tombstone map, for which TokenOwner returns ErrTokenNotFound. Revoke therefore returns the idempotent success immediately and never reaches DeleteRefresh - the one place that clears the tombstone, whose own comment says 'an explicit revocation of a spent token says the replay signal is no longer wanted for that value'. So the documented pop behaviour is dead code for spent refresh values in MemoryStore. Two consequences: (1) a caller that explicitly revokes a rotated/old refresh token is told 'revoked' while the tombstone stays armed, so a later presentation of that value produces a spurious *RefreshReuseError and revokes descendants (see S01-3); (2) revoking a refresh value does not revoke the still-live descendants of its family even though the family id is available in the tombstone.
findings.exploit: A client that keeps its previous refresh token and calls RFC 7009 revocation on it (a plausible cleanup after rotation) receives 200 OK. The consumed token's tombstone remains; when that value is next presented - by the client retrying, or by an attacker who captured it - MemoryStore reports reuse and the server revokes the whole family, including the client's current live refresh token.
findings.recommendation: Have MemoryStore.TokenOwner also resolve spent values to their tombstone's ClientID (so owner comparison works), and let Revoke's DeleteRefresh clear the tombstone as documented. If TokenOwner must stay a pure 'live token' read (the current comment asks for that), add an explicit tombstone-aware revocation path and correct the DeleteRefresh/Revoke comments so the dead branch is not advertised.

findings.title: Audit failures are silently discarded, so reuse detection, revocation and failed exchanges can go unrecorded
findings.why: Every security-relevant event in the service funnels through record: oauth.authorize, oauth.exchange_failed, oauth.reuse_detected (the RFC 9700 theft signal), oauth.token, oauth.revoke, oauth.grant.revoke and the device events. The error is explicitly discarded with '_, so a failing or back-pressured audit sink produces a completely silent gap: the destructive family revocation still happens, but the operator has no record that it happened or why. For oauth.reuse_detected this defeats the purpose of the event, since the whole point of detection is to give an operator something to act on.
findings.exploit: A compromised or overloaded audit sink (or a deliberately jammed one) stops receiving events while token issuance and family revocation continue normally. An attacker who triggers theft-signal revocations can do so without leaving the corresponding audit trail, and incident response has no timeline.
findings.recommendation: Do not discard the error: at minimum log it at error level with the action, or return it on the paths where the audit is part of the security guarantee (reuse_detected, revoke, grant revoke). If audit is best-effort by design, record the drop in a counter and log it once per failure so the gap is observable.

findings.title: Client secrets are stored as an unsalted SHA-256 digest, so a weak config-file secret is off-line crackable if the store leaks
findings.why: Client secrets are compared through a plain, unsalted, single-round SHA-256. The token store justifies this for access/refresh tokens because those are 32 random bytes with nothing to brute-force; client secrets have no such guarantee. The admin path generates high-entropy secrets (internal/admin/admin.go newSecret) so those are fine, but configuredClient builds a client directly from [client].clientSecret in the operator's config file, which may be any string. If the registry's secretHash column is ever disclosed (DB dump, backup, log), a low-entropy configured secret can be recovered with commodity hardware and then used to impersonate the client at the token/revoke endpoints. The same digest also makes the client secret equal at rest to TokenHash, so the codebase has one hash for both credentials despite different entropy assumptions.
findings.exploit: An operator sets a memorable client secret in the config (e.g. a project name plus a year). An attacker who obtains the client row (via the persistent registry or a leaked backup) brute-forces the unsalted SHA-256 in hours and authenticates as that confidential client, obtaining tokens for every user it has grants for and revoking others' tokens through the client-authenticated endpoints.
findings.recommendation: Hash client secrets with a salted, slow KDF (bcrypt/argon2/scrypt) or at least a per-client random salt prepended to a SHA-256, stored alongside the digest; keep NewSecretHash for the high-entropy generated secrets only if a versioned hash format distinguishes the two. Enforce a minimum length/entropy when loading [client].clientSecret.

findings.title: MemoryStore serialises all token operations on one Mutex and scans every record under the lock, so account-page reads and sweeps block token introspection
findings.evidence:
type MemoryStore struct {
	mu      sync.Mutex
	codes   map[string]AuthorizationCode
	access  map[string]AccessToken
	refresh map[string]RefreshToken
findings.why: The store uses a single sync.Mutex (not RWMutex) and holds it across whole-map scans. SweepExpired iterates all four maps while locked; ListBySubject scans every access and refresh record for one subject; DeleteBySubjectClient and RevokeTokens walk every map. Every GetAccess - which is on the hot path of every bearer-authenticated request through oauth.Introspect and httpapi's withBearer - contends on the same lock. In a memory-store deployment, one user opening the grants page or one janitor sweep turns into an O(total tokens) critical section that stalls all token reads and writes, so the cost of a page load grows with global token count rather than with the user's own grants.
findings.exploit: A single authenticated subject with a modest number of grants repeatedly calls GET /v1/grants while the token store is large; each call holds the global mutex for a full scan, serialising introspections for the whole process. Because this is the documented non-durable store, the impact is bounded to deployments that use it, but the amplification is unbounded in token count.
findings.recommendation: Use sync.RWMutex so read paths do not exclude each other, and index tokens by subject (or subject+client) so ListBySubject/DeleteBySubjectClient do not scan all records under the lock. Make SweepExpired incremental (bounded work per call) so a janitor pass cannot monopolise the lock.

findings.title: Store reads return struct copies whose Scopes slices alias the stored backing array, so a caller mutating a returned record corrupts stored authorization state
findings.why: The maps store structs by value but the Scopes field is a slice header; copying the struct copies the header, not the backing array. GetAccess/GetCode/GetRefresh/ConsumeRefresh/ConsumeCode all return that header, and oauth.Introspect forwards it directly as TokenInfo.Scopes (as.go:374) into a publicly consumed result. GrantRecord.Scopes is built the same way in ListBySubject. No current caller mutates the returned slice, so this is latent rather than exploited, but the public Service/Store API hands out a writable alias to the store's own record: any future caller (an in-place scope filter, a sort, an append that fits capacity) would silently rewrite the scopes of a live token or authorization code in the store, changing what the token authorizes.
findings.exploit: Not reachable through the current oauth/ consumers. A future or third-party consumer of oauth.Service.Introspect or oauth.Store.GetAccess that does info.Scopes[0] = ... or sort.Slice(info.Scopes, ...) changes the stored record's scopes without any store write, so a token could be widened or narrowed at a distance; family/ownership checks would still pass.
findings.recommendation: Return defensive copies of Scopes on every store read (append([]Scope(nil), t.Scopes...)), or document the aliasing contract on Store and make the stores share an immutable value type. Cloning on read is cheap relative to the SHA-256 already performed per lookup.

findings.title: The declared-length pre-check is the only path to 413; a chunked body over the cap surfaces as a 400 malformed-form instead
findings.why: The size cap itself is enforced for every body (MaxBytesReader caps the reads), so this is not a bypass. The contract is only that a caller can distinguish 'too large' by error. For a chunked or Content-Length:-1 request the pre-check is skipped and the overrun is reported to the handler as a read error from ParseForm; upstreamkit's handleToken/handleRevoke turn that into 400 invalid_request 'malformed form body' rather than 413 'request body too large', and httpapi's JSON routes similarly return 400 malformed JSON. A client that relies on the documented 413 to decide whether to retry with a smaller body instead retries the same oversized chunked request. The comment acknowledges the chunked case but not that the resulting error shape changes.
findings.exploit: A client (or a proxy in front of it) sends a Transfer-Encoding: chunked body larger than 64 KiB. The cap holds, but the response is 400/invalid_request rather than the documented 413, so the client cannot tell a body-size problem from a malformed request.
findings.recommendation: Have the consumers detect http.MaxBytesError (errors.As(err, new(*http.MaxBytesError))) around ParseForm/decode and map it to the same 413 shape the declared-length path produces, or have LimitFormBody wrap r.Body in a reader that converts the overflow into ErrBodyTooLarge the handler already knows.

notes: Round-9 independent pass; no AUDIT-ISSUES.md, docs/security-audit-*, internal/zzprobe/**, _audit/**, audit/** or scratchpad/** was read as a source of conclusions. Contract observations were confirmed by reading the sibling Postgres oauth.Store implementation (contrast for S01-3/S01-5) and by reading test files only to confirm invariants, never as the origin of a claim. No Docker/Postgres available, so the Postgres store behaviour (tombstone deadline, AtomicAPI) is established from source, not execution. oauth.Service is transport-agnostic; the highest-value untrusted-input flows in the Re0Auth OP live in internal/oidchttp (a separate engine) and in upstreamkit, so the oauth-core findings here are mostly invariant/contract defects plus the device-grant and cascade-auth issues. The device grant methods (oauth/device.go) are not in the stated primary file list but are production files in the oauth/ scope; they are included for completeness and can be de-duplicated if another round owns the device flow. Findings S01-1 and S01-3 depend on no external sweep being run; the package explicitly permits that configuration, and the Postgres sibling does not share the defect, which is what makes the divergence a finding rather than a documented tradeoff. Uncertain: S01-3's real-world victim requires a live descendant generation in the same family at the moment an expired tombstone is replayed; S01-6's impact depends on the embedder's CascadeRevoke hook. No critical-severity issue was found in this scope.
